When I asked him to provide me detail, he could not tell me much more than the fact that he has trouble with his walking and that he has trouble with his bladder.  He is vaguely aware that he has trouble with his memory.,According to his family, he has had difficulty with his gait for at least three or four years.  At first, they thought it was weakness and because of he was on the ground (for example, gardening) he was not able to get up by himself.  They did try stopping the statin that he was taking at that time, but because there was no improvement over two weeks, they resumed the statin.  As time progressed, he developed more and more difficulty.  He started to shuffle.  He started using a cane about two and a half years ago and has used a walker with wheels in the front since July of 2006.  At this point, he frequently if not always has trouble getting in or out of the seat.  He frequently tends to lean backwards or sideways when sitting.  He frequently if not always has trouble getting in or out a car, always shuffles or scuffs his feet, always has trouble turning or changing direction, always has trouble with uneven surfaces or curbs, and always has to hold on to someone or something when walking.  He has not fallen in the last month.  He did fall earlier, but there seemed to be fewer opportunities for him to fall.  His family has recently purchased a lightweight wheelchair to use if he is traveling long distances.  He has no stairs in his home, however, his family indicates that he would not be able to take stairs.  His handwriting has become smaller and shakier.,In regard to the bladder, he states, "I wet the bed."  In talking with his family, it seems as if he has no warning that he needs to empty his bladder.  He was diagnosed with a small bladder tumor in 2005.  This was treated by Dr. Y.  Dr. X does not think that the bladder tumor has anything to do with the patient's urinary incontinence.  The patient has worn a pad or undergarment for at least one to one and a half years.  His wife states that they go through two or three of them per day.  He has been placed on medications; however, they have not helped.,He has no headaches or sensation of head fullness.,In regard to the thinking and memory, at first he seemed forgetful and had trouble with dates.  Now he seems less spontaneous and his family states he seems to have trouble expressing himself.  His wife took over his medications about two years ago.  She stopped his driving about three years ago.  She discovered that his license had been expired for about a year and she was concerned enough at that time that she told him he could drive no more.  Apparently, he did not object.  At this point, he frequently has trouble with memory, orientation, and everyday problems solving at home.  He needs coaching for his daily activities such as reminders to brush his teeth, put on his clothes, and so forth.  He is a retired office machine repairman.  He is currently up and active about 12 hours a day and sleeping or lying down about 12 hours per day.,He has not had PT or OT and has not been treated with medications for Parkinson's disease or Alzheimer's disease.  He has been treated for the bladder.  He has not had lumbar puncture.,Past medical history and review of all 14 systems from the form they completed for this visit that I reviewed with them is negative with the exception that he has had hypertension since 1985, hypercholesterolemia since 1997, and diabetes since 1998.  The bladder tumor was discovered in 2005 and was treated noninvasively.  He has lost weight from about 200 pounds to 180 pounds over the last two or three years.  He had a period of depression in 1999 and was on Prozac for a while, but this was then stopped.  He used to drink a significant amount of alcohol.  This was problematic enough that his wife was concerned.  She states he stopped when she retired and she was at home all day.,SOCIAL HISTORY:  ,He quit smoking in 1968.  His current weight is 183 pounds.  His tallest height is 5 feet 10 inches.,FAMILY HISTORY:  ,His grandfather had arthritis.  His father had Parkinson's disease.  His mother had heart disease and a sister has diabetes.,He does not have a Living Will and indicates he would wish his wife to make decisions for him if he could not make them for himself.,REVIEW OF HYDROCEPHALUS RISK FACTORS: , None.,ALLERGIES: , None.,MEDICATIONS: , Metformin 500 mg three times a day, Lipitor 10 mg per day, lisinopril 20 mg per day, metoprolol 50 mg per day, Uroxatral 10 mg per day, Detrol LA 4 mg per day, and aspirin 81 mg per day.,PHYSICAL EXAM: , On examination today, this is a pleasant 76-year-old man who is guided back from the clinic waiting area walking with his walker.  He is well developed, well nourished, and kempt.,Vital Signs:  His weight is 180 pounds.,Head:  The head is normocephalic and atraumatic.  The head circumference is 59 cm, which is the ,75-90th percentile for an adult man whose height is 178 cm.,Spine:  The spine is straight and not tender.  I can easily palpate the spinous processes.  There is no scoliosis.,Skin:  No neurocutaneous stigmata.,Cardiovascular Examination:  No carotid or vertebral bruits.,Mental Status:  Assessed for orientation, recent and remote memory, attention span, concentration, language, and fund of knowledge.  The Mini-Mental State Exam score was 17/30.  He did not know the year, season, or day of the week nor did he know the building or specialty or the floor.  There was a tendency for perseveration during the evaluation.  He could not copy the diagram of intersecting pentagons.,Cranial Nerve Exam:  No evidence of papilledema.  The pupillary light reflex is intact as are extraocular movements without nystagmus, facial expression and sensation, hearing, head turning, tongue, and palate movement.,Motor Exam:  Normal bulk and strength, but the tone is marked by significant paratonia.  There is no atrophy, fasciculations, or drift.  There is tremulousness of the outstretched hands.,Sensory Exam:  Is difficult to interpret.  Either he does not understand the test or he is mostly guessing.,Cerebellar Exam:  Is intact for finger-to-nose, heel-to-knee, and rapid alternating movement tests.  There is no dysarthria.,Reflexes:  Trace in the arms, 2+ at the knees, and 0 at the ankles.  It is not certain whether there is a Babinski sign or simply withdrawal.,Gait:  Assessed using the Tinetti assessment tool that shows a balance score of 7-10/16 and a gait score of 2-5/12 for a total score of 9-15/28, which is significantly impaired.,REVIEW OF X-RAYS: , I personally reviewed the MRI scan of the brain from December 11, 2007 at Advanced Radiology.  It shows the ventricles are enlarged with a frontal horn span of 5.0 cm.  The 3rd ventricle contour is flat.  The span is enlarged at 12 mm.  The sylvian aqueduct is patent.  There is a pulsation artifact.  The corpus callosum is effaced.  There are extensive T2 signal abnormalities that are confluent in the corona radiata.  There are also scattered T2 abnormalities in the basal ganglia.  There is a suggestion of hippocampal atrophy.  There is also a suggestion of vermian atrophy.,

llm_plan:
### ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

**ASSESSMENT:**  
1. **Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH)**: This 76-year-old man presents with the classic clinical triad of progressive gait disturbance (shuffling, imbalance, postural instability, Tinetti score 9-15/28, cane/walker dependence over 3-4 years), urinary incontinence (nocturnal enuresis without urgency, refractory to Detrol/Uroxatral, 1-1.5 years), and subcortical dementia (MMSE 17/30 with disorientation, memory impairment, perseveration, poor visuospatial function, executive dysfunction requiring cues for ADLs). MRI confirms ventriculomegaly disproportionate to cortical atrophy (frontal horn span 5.0 cm, flat/enlarged 3rd ventricle at 12 mm, effaced corpus callosum, patent aqueduct without obstruction), consistent with hydrocephalus ex-vacuo or communicating hydrocephalus. No hydrocephalus risk factors (trauma, infection, SAH). Symptoms progressive without PD/AD treatment or PT/OT. Highest suspicion for iNPH; positive response to CSF removal would support.  
2. **Cerebrovascular disease (small vessel ischemic disease)**: Extensive confluent periventricular corona radiata and basal ganglia T2/FLAIR hyperintensities on MRI, likely contributing to gait/cognitive symptoms (vascular parkinsonism or Binswanger subcortical encephalopathy); risk factors include longstanding HTN, DM, hyperlipidemia, remote heavy EtOH use.  
3. **Dementia, multifactorial (subcortical/vascular ± neurodegenerative)**: MMSE 17/30 with prominent executive/memory/orientation deficits, paratonia, action tremor, micrographia; family hx PD (father) raises possibility of atypical parkinsonism (e.g., vascular or DLB), but no resting tremor, asymmetry, or gaze palsy. Hippocampal/vermian atrophy suggests possible comorbid AD or cerebellar degeneration.  
4. **Urinary incontinence, likely neurogenic (NPH-related)**: Refractory to anticholinergics/alfuzosin; remote noninvasive bladder tumor treatment unlikely causative.  
5. **Comorbidities**: HTN, T2DM, hyperlipidemia (controlled on meds); remote depression, remote heavy EtOH/smoking (quit). No acute issues.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Diagnostic/therapeutic trial for NPH**:  
   - Proceed with **large-volume lumbar puncture (LP) today** (40-50 mL CSF removal) by interventional radiology or fluoroscopy-guided if needed. Pre-LP: baseline Tinetti gait/balance score, MMSE, timed up-and-go, and bladder symptom assessment (with family input). Repeat immediately post-LP and at 1-4 hours. Measure opening pressure. Send CSF for cell count, protein/glucose, Gram stain/culture, oligoclonal bands, and 14-3-3 (rule out infection/inflammation/CJD). Contraindications reviewed (no coagulopathy).  
   - If ≥20-30% improvement in gait/cognition/bladder: high likelihood of shunt responsiveness.  

2. **Neurosurgical referral**: Urgent consult post-LP for ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt evaluation if tap test positive (programmable valve preferred). Discuss risks (infection, hemorrhage, overdrainage).  

3. **Rehabilitation**:  
   - **PT referral**: Urgent, for gait/balance training, fall prevention, walker optimization.  
   - **OT referral**: For ADLs, home safety evaluation, adaptive equipment (e.g., wheelchair use).  

4. **Medications**:  
   - **No changes to current regimen** (metformin 500 mg TID, Lipitor 10 mg qd, lisinopril 20 mg qd, metoprolol 50 mg qd, Uroxatral 10 mg qd, Detrol LA 4 mg qd, ASA 81 mg qd). Optimize vascular risk (target BP <130/80, A1c <7, LDL <70).  
   - Trial **donepezil 5 mg PO qhs** (titrate to 10 mg after 4 weeks if tolerated) for cognitive symptoms; monitor for GI effects, bradycardia.  
   - Hold **levodopa trial** for now (low suspicion for PD; re-evaluate post-LP/shunt).  

5. **Laboratory/imaging**:  
   - **STAT labs post-LP** as above.  
   - Routine: CBC, CMP, HbA1c, lipid panel, TSH, B12/folate, RPR (today, if not recent).  
   - **No additional imaging** unless LP contraindicated or negative response (consider DaTscan if parkinsonism prominent post-LP).  

6. **Referrals/consults**:  
   - **Urology**: f/u as needed for bladder tumor surveillance ± urodynamics post-NPH treatment.  
   - **Neuropsychology**: Formal testing after LP/shunt to quantify deficits.  

7. **Patient education/counseling**: Discuss NPH diagnosis, shunt option (50-80% improvement rate in responders), fall risks (no driving, home mods), advance directives (wife as surrogate). Provide NPH handout.  

8. **Follow-up**: Return in 1 week post-LP (or sooner if complications) with family to review results and repeat neuro exam. Telephone update same day post-LP. If shunt placed, f/u 1 month post-op.

### ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

**ASSESSMENT:**  
11-month-old male with low/intermediate-risk neuroblastoma (initial stage 2, left adrenal primary s/p gross total resection at 6 weeks of age; subsequent right adrenal mass biopsied consistent with second primary/metastasis, favorable Shimada histology, non-N-Myc amplified). Currently receiving multi-agent chemotherapy per COG protocol P9641 (off-study; cycle 2 completed 05/21/07 with carboplatin, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin). Post-chemotherapy neutropenia resolved with G-CSF support (ANC now 2974). Interval mild URI (nasal congestion) resolving without fever or ill appearance; oral thrush resolved after fluconazole restart. Mild chemotherapy-related effects including anemia (Hgb 10.9), mild transaminitis (AST 51), and borderline hypertension (BP 135/74, elevated for age). Well-nourished with appropriate growth (wt 10.5 kg ~50th percentile, ht 76.8 cm ~75th percentile for age); no evidence of disease progression on exam (no organomegaly or palpable masses). Family stressors ongoing with parental separation/divorce.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Chemotherapy:** Continue P9641 regimen. Hold G-CSF now that ANC >1500 and stable (wean to every other day if ANC drops below 1000; discontinue when ANC >1500 x 3 days off G-CSF). Schedule cycle 3 when ANC >1000, Hgb >8, platelets >100k (target early next week; obtain pre-chemo CBC/diff/plt on 05/30/07).  
2. **Supportive Medications:**  
   - Continue Bactrim 32 mg PO BID Fri-Sun (PCP prophylaxis).  
   - Fluconazole 37.5 mg PO daily x 7 more days (thrush resolved clinically; recheck oral exam).  
   - Zofran 1.5 mg PO q6h PRN nausea.  
3. **Laboratory Tests:**  
   - Repeat CBC/diff/plt, CMP (including LFTs) today and Monday 05/28/07 to guide G-CSF wean and cycle 3 timing.  
   - Urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA) today for disease surveillance.  
4. **Imaging/Radiologic Studies:**  
   - Abdominal/pelvic MRI (no contrast if possible) within 2 weeks to reassess right adrenal mass size/response post-cycle 2.  
   - Consider MIBG scan post-cycle 4 per protocol for full staging if not recent.  
5. **Hypertension Evaluation:** Recheck BP today in all 4 extremities (manual cuff) and obtain 24-hour ambulatory BP monitor if confirmed >95th percentile for age/height. If persistent, obtain renal US and echo; cardiology consult if >99th percentile. Hold NSAIDs if needed.  
6. **Other:**  
   - Nutrition consult if appetite remains poor (supplemental feeds if wt velocity declines).  
   - Social work consult for family support (parental divorce/custody stressors impacting care coordination).  
7. **Follow-up:** Return in 1 week (06/01/07) with labs for chemo clearance; supervised by Dr. X. Call sooner if fever >38.5°C, poor PO intake, or new symptoms.

Exam shows distal sensory deficits (absent L toe vibration, diminished R; LT/temp loss to knees), mild head/arm tremor, few bilateral calf fasciculations, and wide-based gait with L toe weakness. Cervical MRI demonstrates multilevel spondylosis with severe C5-6 foraminal narrowing/borderline cord compression and C6-7 mild foraminal narrowing/left paracentral borderline cord compression, likely contributing to neck pain and possibly hand symptoms/gait (though minimal UMN signs). Distal sensory-predominant polyneuropathy is favored etiology of lower extremity sensory loss/gait ataxia (normal B12/B1, low-normal B6, good DM control on Actos/HbA1c 6.0, but Crohn's/malabsorption as contributor); EMG/NCS needed to confirm and exclude concurrent radiculopathy/myopathy (mild CPK elevation, fasciculations). Fatigue most bothersome, likely multifactorial (suboptimally treated depression on Lexapro 20mg, CPAP non-compliance for OSA, possible anemia/sedentary state); mild recall deficit noted but prior formal cognitive testing normal. No evidence of ALS (normal strength/reflexes/coordination), paraproteinemia (SPEP abnormal but immunofixation neg), active inflammation (normal ESR/CRP), or surgical myelopathy (per recent neurosurg eval). Differential includes sensory neuropathy (DM/Crohn's), cervical spondylotic myelopathy/radiculopathy, and depression/OSA-related fatigue; malignancy/infection unlikely given chronicity/normal labs/imaging.

### ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

**ASSESSMENT:**  
76-year-old female with advanced Alzheimer's dementia presenting with acute worsening of baseline cognitive impairment and altered mental status (AMS) following a mechanical fall with head strike on wheelchair (no LOC). Exam notable for garbled/inappropriate speech, poor cooperation with commands, but intact focal motor/sensory function, symmetric DTRs, and no drift. Negative head CT (rules out acute ICH/subdural/hemorrhage) and C-spine CT (rules out acute fracture). Multifactorial delirium likely, with contributors including:  
1. **Hyperkalemia (K 5.9)**: Symptomatic contributor to AMS; etiology unclear (meds? renal? hemolysis? rhabdo post-fall?).  
2. **Leukopenia (WBC 3.8) with left shift (8% bands)**: Concerning for occult infection (e.g., UTI, skin source from excoriations, aspiration pneumonia) despite no fever or focal signs; relative neutropenia.  
3. **Baseline Alzheimer's + possible medication effects**: Subtherapeutic valproic acid level (24.3, below typical 50-100 mcg/mL therapeutic range for neuro/psych indications), supratherapeutic INR (1.92) on chronic Coumadin (fall risk). No evidence of ACS (normal troponin), stroke, or metabolic derangements otherwise (normal Mg). Differential also includes occult subdural (rarely seen early on non-con CT), postictal state, or metabolic encephalopathy.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Admission**: Medicine floor (or observation if stabilizes rapidly) for close neuro monitoring q4h, serial mental status exams, and delirium workup. Fall precautions, bedside sitter if needed. D/C C-collar after repeat neuro/C-spine exam confirms no deficits.  
2. **Laboratory tests**:  
   - STAT repeat CMP (electrolytes, BUN/Cr, glucose), CBC w/ diff, CPK (rhabdo), lactate.  
   - UA/UCx, blood cultures x2 (occult sepsis workup).  
   - Repeat INR/PT; VPA level (trend).  
3. **Imaging studies**:  
   - CXR (rule out pneumonia/aspiration).  
   - EKG (hyperkalemia changes; q6-8h until K normal).  
4. **Medications**:  
   - **Hyperkalemia**: LOCA regimen (kayexalate 30g PO/NG q6h x3, insulin 10U IV + D50 1U push, NS 500mL bolus then 100mL/hr; recheck K q2-4h). No K supplements.  
   - Hold Coumadin (recheck INR daily; resume if <1.5 and no bleed). No reversal at this time (no active bleed).  
   - Continue valproic acid (monitor level; consider dose adjustment if ongoing AMS).  
   - Delirium: Haloperidol 0.5mg IV q6h PRN severe agitation (avoid benzos). Acetaminophen 650mg q6h PRN pain.  
   - Skin: Mupirocin oint to excoriations BID; diphenhydramine 25mg PO qHS PRN itch (caution sedation).  
5. **Consultations/Referrals**:  
   - Neurology consult for AMS/delirium evaluation (possible EEG if seizures suspected).  
   - Social work for Alzheimer's support/discharge planning.  
6. **Procedures**: None acute.  
7. **Follow-up**: Reassess AMS q4-6h; if improves and workup negative, discharge in 24-48h to baseline living situation with PCP f/u in 1 week. If no improvement in 24h, consider MRI brain or LP (if infection/CJD concern). Family education on fall prevention, med reconciliation.

### ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

**ASSESSMENT:**  
1. **Recurrent malignant meningioma with disease progression and leptomeningeal recurrence:** Confirmed by serial MRIs (summer 2007 through recent study), showing interval growth along brain surface with associated mass effect and extensive peritumoral edema. This correlates with clinical decline including right hemiparesis, expressive dysphasia, confusion, seizures, and profound functional impairment (non-ambulatory, dependent ADLs). History of two prior resections (07/2006 and 08/2007) followed by radiation supports aggressive biology refractory to local therapies.  
2. **Symptomatic brain edema:** Contributing to neurologic deficits and hyperventilation episodes; currently on high-dose dexamethasone with partial symptom control.  
3. **Seizure disorder:** Controlled on dual therapy (levetiracetam and phenytoin) but with recent history of breakthrough seizures requiring hospitalization.  
4. **Recent Clostridium difficile infection:** Likely hospital-acquired, treated with metronidazole; resolution uncertain.  
5. **Multimorbidity with poor performance status:** Right hemiparesis, dependency, nursing home residence, and opioid requirements limit aggressive interventions; goals-of-care discussion warranted given poor prognosis.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Medications (adjustments):**  
   - Continue **dexamethasone 6 mg PO/IV QID** (total 24 mg/day) for cerebral edema; add **ondansetron 4-8 mg PO/IV q6-8h PRN nausea** and monitor for steroid side effects (hyperglycemia, GI bleed). Plan slow taper (e.g., 2 mg BID reduction q3-5 days) once stable, targeting lowest effective dose.  
   - **Levetiracetam (Keppra) 1500 mg PO BID**: Continue (therapeutic).  
   - **Phenytoin (Dilantin) 300 mg PO daily**: Continue but check level today; target 10-20 mcg/mL; adjust dose if subtherapeutic.  
   - **Metronidazole (Flagyl) 500 mg PO TID**: Complete 10-14 day course for C. diff; recheck stool studies post-treatment.  
   - **Oxycodone 5-10 mg PO q4-6h PRN pain**: Continue; consider transition to long-acting opioid (e.g., oxycodone ER 10 mg BID) if chronic needs.  
   - **Pantoprazole (Protonix) 40 mg PO daily** (switch from Prilosec for better steroid ulcer prophylaxis).  
   - **Aspirin 81 mg PO daily**: Continue for cardioprotection.  
   - Discontinue oxygen if SpO2 stable >92% on room air.  

2. **Laboratory tests:**  
   - STAT: CBC, CMP (incl. glucose, LFTs), phenytoin level, magnesium.  
   - Today: C. diff toxin PCR, INR (if any coagulopathy risk).  
   - Weekly monitoring of CBC/CMP while on high-dose steroids.  

3. **Imaging studies:**  
   - No immediate new imaging; recent MRI sufficient. Repeat brain MRI with/without contrast in 4-6 weeks to assess edema response or if clinical worsening.  

4. **Consultations/Referrals:**  
   - **Palliative care/Neuro-oncology**: Urgent today for goals-of-care discussion, symptom management, and trial of bevacizumab (e.g., 10 mg/kg IV q2 weeks) for refractory edema if performance status allows (ECOG ≤2).  
   - **Radiation oncology**: Evaluate for re-irradiation (e.g., SRS or WBRT) or gamma knife if focal progression.  
   - **Neurology**: For seizure optimization if levels suboptimal.  
   - **PT/OT/Speech therapy**: In nursing home for maintenance rehab focusing on safety and ADLs.  
   - **Hospice evaluation**: If declines further interventions.  

5. **Procedures:**  
   - None acute. Consider VP shunt if hydrocephalus develops.  

6. **Follow-up:**  
   - Clinic follow-up in 1 week (or sooner if worsening neuro status).  
   - Nursing home to monitor VS q shift, neuro checks q4h, daily weights, and strict I/Os. Family education on signs of deterioration (e.g., increased lethargy, seizures). Advance directives discussed.  

Prognosis guarded; focus on quality of life and symptom control. Discussed with patient/family (limited capacity noted).

**ASSESSMENT AND PLAN**

**ASSESSMENT:**  
60-year-old female with chronic low back pain and right sciatica/buttock pain in the setting of multilevel lumbar degenerative disc disease (DDD), moderate central canal stenosis at L4-L5, and possible right L5-S1 foraminal synovial cyst or soft tissue mass causing nerve root displacement per 2007 lumbar MRI (significantly outdated). Right hip pain with positive Patrick/FABER test and pain on rotation suggests intra-articular hip pathology (e.g., osteoarthritis, labral tear, or femoroacetabular impingement); left buttock zinging on deep palpation raises concern for S1 radiculopathy but without corroborating MRI findings or positive straight leg raise. Additional complaints include chronic headaches (likely migraine or tension-type, exacerbated by frequent Fiorinal use with risk of medication overuse headache and barbiturate dependence), polyarthralgias with stiffness and reduced ROM consistent with osteoarthritis, new heart murmur (etiology unclear, ?functional vs. valvular), sore throat (viral vs. bacterial), stable hypothyroidism, hypercholesterolemia, and anemia. Recent 6 lb weight gain without other red flags. No evidence of cauda equina, myelopathy, or inflammatory/rheumatologic process. Family history notable for multiple cancers warrants age-appropriate screening.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Symptom Management:**  
   - **Pain (back/hip/joints):** Start naproxen 500 mg PO BID with PPI (omeprazole 20 mg qd) for gastroprotection x 2 weeks PRN; trial acetaminophen 1000 mg q6h PRN (max 3 g/day) as adjunct. Taper Fiorinal to PRN only (<2x/week) over 2 weeks to avoid rebound; if inadequate, consider gabapentin 300 mg qHS, titrate to 300 mg TID PRN neuropathic pain.  
   - **Headaches:** Add topiramate 25 mg qHS, titrate to 100 mg BID if persistent; consider sumatriptan 50-100 mg PRN acute (max 200 mg/day).  
   - **Sore throat:** Rapid strep test in clinic; if positive, amoxicillin 500 mg BID x 10 days; otherwise supportive (lozenges, hydration).  

2. **Laboratory Tests:**  
   - CBC with differential (anemia workup), TSH/free T4 (hypothyroidism optimization), comprehensive metabolic panel, lipid panel, ESR/CRP (rule out inflammatory arthropathy), vitamin D level (joint pain), B12/folate (anemia).  

3. **Imaging Studies:**  
   - Review patient-provided hip/knee radiographs; if not diagnostic, order right hip MRI (with/without contrast, non-contrast if dye allergy limits) to evaluate for labral pathology or OA.  
   - Repeat lumbar spine MRI without contrast (due to Hypaque allergy) to assess progression of stenosis/synovial cyst and correlate with symptoms.  

4. **Referrals/Consultations:**  
   - Orthopedics (hip/low back) within 4 weeks for further evaluation +/- injections (e.g., hip intra-articular steroid or lumbar ESI at L5-S1 if MRI confirms).  
   - Cardiology for heart murmur: outpatient echocardiogram and EKG referral within 2 weeks.  
   - PT evaluation for core strengthening, hip/back mobilization, and gait training; start within 1 week x 6-8 weeks.  
   - Rheumatology if labs suggest inflammatory process.  

5. **Procedures:** None acutely; consider fluoroscopic lumbar ESI or hip injection by ortho/pain if imaging confirmatory.  

6. **Medications/Supplements Review:** Continue Levoxyl 75 mcg qd, Lexapro 20 mg qd, Prempro qd (discuss risks/benefits given family cancer hx; consider DEXA scan for bone health). Hold policosanol (limited evidence, ?interferes with lipids); continue other supplements but consolidate (e.g., multivitamin covers many); recheck lipids after 6 weeks. Aspirin PRN ok for cardioprotection.  

7. **Screening/Counseling:**  
   - Mammogram and colonoscopy overdue (last 1989 biopsy, 2007 scope); refer for both.  
   - Depression screen (PHQ-9); social work for home support given isolation.  
   - Lifestyle: Weight management (low-carb diet, 30 min walking 5x/week), smoking cessation counseling (though denies).  

**Follow-up:** Return in 2 weeks to review labs/imaging, assess pain response, and adjust plan; sooner if worsening neuro symptoms (e.g., weakness, incontinence). Call for urgent issues.

History related to this illness probably dates back to October of 2006 when he had onset of swelling and discomfort in the left testicle with what he described as a residual "lump" posteriorly.  The left testicle has continued to be painful off and on since.  In early November, he developed pain in the posterior part of his upper right leg, which he initially thought was related to skateboarding and muscle strain.  Physical therapy was prescribed and the discomfort temporarily improved.  In December, he noted onset of increasing fatigue.  He used to work out regularly, lifting lifts, doing abdominal exercises, and playing basketball and found he did not have energy to pursue these activities.  He has lost 10 pounds since December and feels his appetite has decreased.  Night sweats and cough began in December, for which he was treated with a course of Augmentin.  However, both of these problems have continued.  He also began taking Accutane for persistent acne in December (this agent was stopped on 02/19/2007).  Despite increasing fatigue and lethargy, he continues his studies at University of Denver, has a biology major (he aspires to be an ophthalmologist).,The morning of 02/19/2007, he awakened with severe right inguinal and right lower quadrant pain. CT scan of the abdomen was obtained to rule out possible appendicitis and on that CT, a large clot in the inferior vena cava extending to the right iliac and femoral veins was found.  He promptly underwent appropriate treatment in interventional radiology with the above-noted angioplasty and placement of a vena caval filter followed by mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis.  Repeat ultrasound there on 02/20/2007 showed no evidence of deep venous thrombosis (DVT).  Continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion was continued.  Because there was no obvious cause of this extensive thrombosis, occult malignancy was suspected.  Appropriate blood studies were obtained and he underwent a PET/CT scan as part of his diagnostic evaluation.  This study showed moderately increased diffuse bone marrow metabolic activity.  Because the WBC continued to rise and showed a preponderance of lymphocytes, the smear was reviewed by pathologist, Sheryl Asplund, M.D., and flow cytometry was performed on the peripheral blood.  These studies became available the afternoon of 02/23/2007, and confirmed the diagnosis of precursor-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia.  The patient was transferred here after stopping of the continuous infusion heparin and receiving a dose of Lovenox 60 mg subcutaneously for further diagnostic evaluation and management of the acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).,ALLERGIES: , NO KNOWN DRUG ALLERGIES. Parents are in good health.  A maternal great-grandmother had a deep venous thrombosis (DVT) of leg in her 40s.  A maternal great-uncle developed leukemia around age 50.  A maternal great-grandfather had bone cancer around age 80.  His paternal grandfather died of colon cancer at age 73, which he had had since age 68.  Adult-onset diabetes is present in distant relatives on both sides.,SOCIAL HISTORY:  ,The patient is a student at the University majoring in biology.  He lives in a dorm there.  His parents live in Breckenridge.  He admits to having smoked marijuana off and on with friends and drinking beer off and on as well.,REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: , He has had emesis off and on related to Vicodin and constipation since 02/19/2007, also related to pain medication.  He has had acne for about two years, which he describes as mild to moderate.  He denied shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headaches, joint pains, rashes, except where he has had dressings applied, and extremity pain except for the right leg pain noted above.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  ,GENERAL:  Alert, cooperative, moderately ill-appearing young man.,VITAL SIGNS:  At the time of admission, pulse was 94, respirations 20, blood pressure 120/62, temperature 98.7, height 171.5 cm, weight 63.04 kg, and pulse oximetry on room air 95%.,HAIR AND SKIN:  Mild facial acne.,HEENT:  Extraocular muscles (EOMs) intact. llm_plan:
### ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

**ASSESSMENT:**  
1. **High-risk precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), newly diagnosed.** Confirmed by peripheral blood flow cytometry demonstrating 64% lymphoblasts with a precursor B-cell immunophenotype. High-risk features include adolescent/young adult age group (>10-30 years), hyperleukocytosis (WBC 25,500/μL with blast predominance), elevated LDH (1925 U/L), hepatosplenomegaly, constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss, night sweats), and possible extramedullary involvement (chronic left testicular discomfort/fullness). Extensive DVT is likely paraneoplastic hypercoagulability from undiagnosed ALL. Bone marrow evaluation pending for full risk stratification (cytogenetics, molecular studies including BCR-ABL, MLL rearrangement).  
2. **Extensive right iliac vein and IVC deep vein thrombosis (DVT), clinically resolved.** Status post urgent interventional radiology intervention (balloon angioplasty, mechanical/pharmacologic thrombolysis, IVC filter placement) on 02/19-20/2007 with confirmatory Doppler ultrasound negative for residual DVT on 02/20/2007. Currently on bridging anticoagulation, but subtherapeutic LMWH level (0.27 U/mL).  
3. **Hepatosplenomegaly.** Mild (each 4 cm below costal margins), attributable to leukemic infiltration.  
4. **Mild left testicular fullness/pain.** Ongoing since 10/2006; possible leukemic involvement (testicular sanctuary site) or unrelated (e.g., prior trauma/epididymitis); requires imaging.  
5. **Supportive issues.** Mild hypocalcemia (8.8 mg/dL) and hypoalbuminemia (3.4 g/dL) likely from disease-related inflammation/catabolism; opioid-induced nausea/constipation; mild acne (recent Accutane exposure); low-grade hypoxia (SpO2 95% RA, likely from splenomegaly/anemia).

**PLAN:**  
**Admission/Disposition:** Admit to inpatient Hematology/Oncology service for urgent workup and treatment initiation. Contact pediatric/adolescent-young adult (AYA) ALL team for co-management (e.g., Children's Oncology Group [COG] high-risk protocol or institutional equivalent such as hyper-CVAD or augmented BFM). Notify interventional radiology re: IVC filter status.  

**Diagnostic Evaluation:**  
1. **Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy** (today): For morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics (karyotype), FISH panel (BCR-ABL t(9;22), MLL rearrangements, ETV6-RUNX1, etc.), molecular studies (PCR for minimal residual disease [MRD] markers if applicable).  
2. **Lumbar puncture** (after platelet transfusion if <50k): Cytology, flow cytometry, CSF protein/glucose to evaluate for CNS involvement (mandatory in ALL).  
3. **Scrotal ultrasound** (today): With Doppler to evaluate left testicle for thrombosis, mass, or infiltration.  
4. **Echocardiogram** (within 24-48h): Baseline cardiac function prior to anthracycline-based chemotherapy.  
5. **Daily labs:** CBC with differential, CMP (monitor TLS: uric acid, LDH, phosphorus, potassium), coags (PT/INR/PTT), fibrinogen, quantitative LMWH anti-Xa level (trough 4h post-dose, target 0.5-1.0 U/mL for treatment), beta-D-dimer. LDH q12h x 24h then daily.  

**Therapeutics:**  
1. **Anticoagulation:** Increase Lovenox to 1 mg/kg SQ q12h (actual body weight 63 kg → ~60-80 mg/dose) with repeat anti-Xa level in 6h to confirm therapeutic range. Hold warfarin (risk of supratherapeutic INR with hepatotoxicity from chemo). Continue until stable on LMWH x 3-6 months minimum, then reassess (long-term due to IVC filter/ALL-associated thrombosis).  
2. **Induction chemotherapy:** Initiate TODAY per high-risk ALL protocol (e.g., COG AALL1131 or institutional pediatric-inspired regimen: vincristine, daunorubicin, prednisone, PEG-asparaginase ± cyclophosphamide/cytarabine). Dose per BSA (1.8 m²). Intrathecal methotrexate with LP.  
3. **Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) prophylaxis:** High risk (high WBC, bulky disease). Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV x1 (if uric acid >8 or rising; uric acid normal now), then allopurinol 300 mg PO/NG daily. Hyperhydration (3L/m²/day D5 1/4 NS + 20-40 mEq KCl/L at 150-200 mL/m²/h) targeting UOP >100 mL/m²/h. Avoid excessive free water.  
4. **Supportive care:**  
   - Transfuse: PRBC to Hgb >8 g/dL if symptomatic; platelets to >10k (or >50k pre-procedure).  
   - Protonix 40 mg IV q24h → transition to PO when tolerating.  
   - Pain/nausea: Continue Vicodin 5 mg/300 mg 1-2 tabs q6h PRN; ondansetron 8 mg IV/PO q8h PRN nausea; senna 2 tabs PO BID + docusate 100 mg PO BID for constipation.  
   - Nutrition: Dietitian consult; consider TPN if poor PO intake (low albumin). Calcium carbonate 500 mg PO TID (monitor corrected Ca).  
   - Infection prophylaxis: Levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h (continue pending neutropenia); acyclovir 400 mg PO BID (HSV/VZV); fluconazole 200 mg PO daily if prolonged steroids. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis with TMP-SMX DS TIW once induction starts. Neutropenic precautions.  
   - Acne: Topical benzoyl peroxide/clindamycin PRN (avoid systemic retinoids).  

**Consults/Referrals:**  
- Pediatric Hematology/Oncology (immediate co-management for AYA ALL protocol).  
- Interventional Radiology (f/u IVC filter/DVT).  
- Urology (if testicular US abnormal).  

**Follow-up:** Daily inpatient rounds with serial labs/imaging as above. Reassess response to induction after Day 7-14 (repeat marrow for MRD). Oncology f/u post-induction for consolidation. Counsel family on prognosis (high-risk ALL cure rates ~60-70% with pediatric regimens), fertility preservation (sperm banking pre-chemo), and social support (dorm/school leave).

### ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

#### ASSESSMENT:
1. **Longstanding insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus (35 years duration)**: Patient with polyuria likely due to hyperglycemia/polyuria from poor glycemic control. On dual therapy with basal insulin and glipizide; recent weight loss (8 lbs over 1 year) may reflect catabolism. Mild asymmetric sensory deficit (RLE > LLE) may represent concurrent distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
2. **Lumbar degenerative disc disease (DDD) with multilevel stenosis (MRI 11/15/2007)**: Severe disc narrowing at L4-L5/L5-S1, moderate central stenosis L4-L5, severe right foraminal stenosis L5-S1 (correlates with RLE sensory changes to pinprick). No motor deficit, radiculopathy, or myelopathy on exam (normal strength, gait, negative SLR). Likely chronic mechanical back pain; symptoms not detailed but MRI brought in suggests ongoing issue.
3. **New grade 1-2 holosystolic murmur**: Likely mitral regurgitation (MR) given location/timing; no overt heart failure (clear lungs, no edema). Asymptomatic on cardiac ROS but requires evaluation in context of family CAD history, age, and DM.
4. **Dyspnea on exertion**: Uses Advair PRN (suggests underlying reactive airways/COPD); lungs clear today, no hypoxia/edema noted.
5. **Prostate cancer in remission**: Post-radiation, PSA 0.01 (excellent); no current issues.
6. **Poor dentition**: Noted on exam; risk for aspiration/infection.
7. **Other**: History of unilateral orchiectomy (benign); low-normal DTRs at ankles (consistent with DM neuropathy); moderate ETOH use; stable weight/BP.

#### PLAN:
1. **Diabetes/polyuria**:
   - Labs today: HbA1c, fasting glucose, CMP (incl. eGFR), UA (r/o UTI), lipid panel.
   - Home glucose log x 1 week (pre/post-prandial, target <180 post-prandial).
   - Continue insulin 20-25u BID and glipizide 5mg TID with meals; titrate insulin based on log (increase by 2-4u if avg >180). D/C glipizide if A1c >9% to simplify regimen/reduce hypo risk.
   - Nutrition consult for low-carb diabetic diet; encourage 30min daily exercise.
   
2. **Lumbar DDD/stenosis/RLE sensory changes**:
   - Conservative Rx: Acetaminophen 650mg q6h PRN pain (max 3g/d); gabapentin 100mg qHS, increase to 300mg TID as tolerated for neuropathic symptoms (monitor for sedation).
   - PT referral: 2-3x/week x 4 weeks (core strengthening, McKenzie extension exercises, gait training).
   - Repeat lumbar MRI w/wo contrast if no improvement in 6 weeks or new weakness/incontinence.
   - Neuro consult if progresses (e.g., weakness, falls).

3. **Holosystolic murmur**:
   - TTE (transthoracic echocardiogram) stat to evaluate regurgitant valve (MR/TR?), EF, chamber sizes.
   - Cardiology referral post-echo if moderate-severe MR or EF <50%.

4. **Dyspnea**:
   - CXR today if not recent.
   - PFTs with bronchodilator challenge.
   - Continue Advair 250/50 mcg 1 puff BID (not PRN); albuterol MDI 2 puffs q4-6h PRN.
   - Pulmonology referral if PFTs obstructive/restrictive.

5. **Poor dentition**:
   - Dental referral urgent (within 2 weeks) for eval/cleaning.

6. **General**:
   - Vaccinations: Confirm Td/Tdap, influenza, pneumococcal (PCV20), shingles up to date.
   - Continue aspirin 81mg qHS (assuming low-dose), cod liver oil, Centrum.
   - D/C lorazepam (stopped; avoid restart unless anxiety recurs).
   - Lifestyle: Limit ETOH to <7 drinks/week; smoking cessation counseling (though denies).
   - **Follow-up**: Return in 2 weeks with labs/glucose log/MRI review; sooner if weakness, chest pain, worsening SOB, or falls. Telehealth ok if stable.

Lumbar degenerative disc disease with multilevel stenosis
New grade 1-2 holosystolic murmur likely mitral regurgitation
Dyspnea on exertion possibly related to reactive airways/COPD

**ASSESSMENT AND PLAN**

**ASSESSMENT:**  
26-year-old G2P1001 at 28 1/7 weeks gestation with acute left lower quadrant abdominal pain, constipation (no bowel movement x 2 weeks with stool palpable in rectal vault), nausea/vomiting, and acute urinary retention (no void x 24 hours due to pain), most likely due to fecal impaction from constipation exacerbating underlying IBS in pregnancy. Mild leukocytosis (WBC 11.1) and exam findings (LLQ tenderness without peritonitis, bilateral lower back tenderness without CVA) raise concern for superimposed UTI/pyelonephritis given PMH of recurrent UTIs; however, UA shows bacteria without pyuria/nitrites, suggesting possible contamination, dehydration (high SG/ketones), or asymptomatic bacteriuria (culture pending). Dehydration likely contributing to N/V (improved from baseline pregnancy symptoms) and ketonuria. No evidence of preterm labor (cervix closed/long/high/posterior, reassuring FHTs with variability, good FM), abruption, or PROM. Polysubstance abuse (hx cocaine, ongoing marijuana, multiple recent +UDS for opioids/benzos/barbiturates) with exam concerning for acute intoxication/withdrawal (sedated appearance, thrashing, track marks, opioid-seeking behavior). Reassuring fetal status.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Admission:** Observe/admit to L&D for monitoring (pain control, fetal surveillance, IV hydration).  
2. **Hydration/Nutrition:** IV NS bolus 1L, then maintenance 125 mL/hr; advance PO with clear liquids → diet as tolerated. D/C home antiemetics if improved (Phenergan/Zofran).  
3. **Constipation/Impaction:**  
   - Fleet enema x1 now (or manual disimpaction if needed).  
   - Colace 100 mg PO TID + Miralax 17g PO daily.  
4. **Pain Control:** Acetaminophen 650-1000 mg PO q6h PRN (max 4g/day); consider ketorolac 15-30 mg IV q6h x24h if no contraindications (monitor renal function/fetal effects). Avoid opioids if possible due to abuse history.  
5. **UTI Evaluation:**  
   - Repeat clean-catch UA + urine culture (straight cath if unable to void).  
   - Hold Macrobid pending culture/sensitivities; if pyuria/WBCs develop or CVA tenderness worsens, start IV ceftriaxone 1g q24h (renal-adjusted).  
6. **Fetal Monitoring:** Continuous EFM x2-4 hours or until stable; formal NST if needed.  
7. **Substance Abuse:**  
   - STAT UDS.  
   - Social work/OB addiction consult today for counseling, toxicology follow-up, and safety planning.  
   - Psychiatry consult if withdrawal/intoxication confirmed.  
8. **No Imaging/Procedures:** Avoid unless deterioration (e.g., limited RUQ US for pyelo if indicated).  
9. **Follow-up:** D/C to home OB (Lyndhurst) within 24-48 hours if improved/stable; f/u OB visit within 1 week with UDS results. RTC ER prn decreased FM, contractions, bleeding, or worsening pain.  

**Signature:** [Your Name], MD  
OB/GYN Attending

**ASSESSMENT:**  
86-year-old frail female with symptomatic L5 vertebral compression fracture (confirmed on plain films and CT with sclerosis/partial healing but incomplete resolution). Persistent lumbosacral back pain despite several months of conservative management (brace, corset, activity modification), without neurologic red flags (no bowel/bladder dysfunction, no focal weakness beyond age-appropriate giveaway strength and hyporeflexia, normal gait). Mild L4-L5 degenerative changes and grade 1 spondylolisthesis noted but less likely primary pain generator. No evidence of instability, infection, or malignancy on imaging. Appropriate candidate for kyphoplasty given refractory pain impacting quality of life in elderly patient with multiple comorbidities (hypothyroidism, HTN, PMR, remote abdominal surgeries).

**PLAN:**  
1. **Procedure:** Proceed with **bilateral L5 kyphoplasty** as discussed with patient; admit to hospital today for same-day procedure under IR/anesthesia guidance. Verify final IR review of recent CT for approach planning.  
2. **Pre-op evaluation:**  
   - Labs: CBC, CMP, PT/PTT/INR, TSH (given hypothyroidism).  
   - EKG (age >85, HTN).  
   - UA. Hold antiplatelets if applicable per guidelines (discuss with anesthesia).  
3. **Medications:**  
   - Continue home medications (hypothyroid, HTN, PMR regimens).  
   - Pain control: Oxycodone 5 mg PO q4-6h PRN breakthrough pain (avoid codeine, opioids with cephalosporin cross-reactivity low risk); acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN (max 3 g/day). Continue back brace.  
   - Peri-procedural: IR to provide local anesthesia/conscious sedation; notify of PCN/cephalosporin allergy.  
4. **Consults:**  
   - Anesthesia pre-op clearance (frail elderly, multiple comorbidities).  
   - No routine cardiology (stable, no active symptoms).  
5. **Post-procedure:** Admit overnight observation for pain control, mobilization. Discharge when tolerating PO, ambulating with PT.  
6. **Follow-up:** Clinic visit 2 weeks post-op for wound check, pain reassessment, repeat lumbar X-rays. If persistent pain, consider PMR flare vs. adjacent segment issues; ortho/spine referral if needed. Activity: Brace x4-6 weeks, PT referral for core strengthening. Patient verbalized understanding, verbal consent obtained.

**ASSESSMENT:**  
13-year-old female with thoracic hyperkyphosis measuring 46 degrees on lateral spine X-ray (borderline increased; normal 20-45 degrees), likely Scheuermann kyphosis given age at presentation (adolescent growth spurt, recent menarche), radiographic Cobb angle measurement, family history of kyphosis (maternal aunt, grandfather, great-grandmother, second cousin suggesting possible genetic predisposition), and clinical findings of round back posture with hamstring tightness on exam. No back pain, neurologic symptoms (intact strength, sensation, symmetric limbs), or signs of congenital/ neuromuscular etiology (no skin lesions, dimpling, tenderness, or paraspinal spasm). Prior orthopedic evaluation recommended observation, consistent with non-progressive or postural component; however, degree warrants monitoring during remaining skeletal growth. Differential includes postural kyphosis (flexibility not fully assessed clinically) vs. early structural Scheuermann's; no evidence of scoliosis on PA views. Unrelated acute otitis media treated with current antibiotics.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Conservative management (first-line given asymptomatic status, <50-degree curve, post-menarche):**  
   - Refer to physical therapy (PT): Focus on postural correction exercises, hamstring/hip flexor stretching, thoracic extension strengthening, and core stabilization. 2-3 sessions/week x 8-12 weeks, then home program.  
   - Patient/parent education: Emphasize upright posture, backpack ergonomics (<15% body weight, worn on both shoulders), avoidance of slouching/prolonged sitting; return precautions for new pain, progression of deformity, or neurologic changes.  

2. **Imaging:**  
   - Repeat standing PA/lateral scoliosis/kyphosis X-rays in 6 months to assess progression (annual if stable); include hyperextension lateral view if available to evaluate flexibility. No MRI indicated at this time (no red flags).  

3. **Medications:**  
   - No new prescriptions. Continue Zyrtec 10 mg daily, Flonase 1 spray each nostril daily, and Ceftin as prescribed for otitis media (complete course; f/u with ENT/PMD if persistent).  

4. **Referrals/Consultations:**  
   - PT as above. No orthopedic or other specialist referral at this time (concurs with prior observation recommendation but adds proactive PT).  

5. **Follow-up:**  
   - Return to clinic in 6 months with repeat X-rays, or sooner PRN symptoms/progression. Transition to adult primary care after skeletal maturity.  

**Time spent: 45 minutes. Patient/parent verbalized understanding, questions answered.**

**ASSESSMENT:**  
Acute urticaria, likely allergic etiology (possible contact exposure to insulation 2 days prior), without anaphylaxis.  
*Reasoning:* Sudden onset of diffuse pruritic, blanching erythematous/maculopapular rash on torso, upper arms, and buttocks, with associated mild tachycardia but no angioedema, respiratory distress, or other systemic symptoms. Rapid improvement following IM epinephrine and diphenhydramine supports histamine-mediated urticarial reaction rather than alternative diagnoses (e.g., viral exanthem, contact dermatitis alone). No fever or other infectious signs. Etiology unclear but temporally related to recent insulation exposure; no identifiable food, medication, or other triggers.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Disposition:** Stable for discharge home in stable condition with wife. ED observation x30 minutes post-treatment; repeat VS and exam reassuring (rash fading, pruritus resolved).  
2. **Medications:**  
   - Cetirizine (Zyrtec) 10 mg PO daily x7 days (non-sedating H1-antihistamine; may repeat next dose PRN pruritus).  
   - Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) 25-50 mg PO q6h PRN pruritus x3 days (max 300 mg/day; caution with sedation/impairment).  
   - Famotidine 20 mg PO BID x7 days (adjunctive H2-blocker for urticaria control).  
   - No steroids needed given rapid improvement and lack of systemic features.  
3. **Laboratory tests:** None at this time (unnecessary for acute urticaria; consider CBC, tryptase if recurrent/severe).  
4. **Imaging/Procedures:** None.  
5. **Referrals/Consults:**  
   - Establish primary care provider (PCP) urgently given no local physician; f/u within 1 week for ongoing eval.  
   - Allergy/immunology referral if urticaria recurs, persists >6 weeks, or new triggers identified.  
6. **Patient Education/Instructions:**  
   - Avoid potential triggers (e.g., insulation, new exposures); no new meds without allergy review.  
   - Return immediately for SOB, swelling (lips/tongue/throat), hives progression, dizziness, or tachycardia.  
   - OTC calamine lotion or cool compresses PRN for residual itch.  
7. **Follow-up:** PCP f/u in 3-7 days or sooner PRN; return to ED if symptoms worsen.

She formerly worked for Veteran's Home as a CNA.  She has had a long drawn out course of treatment for this shoulder.  She tried physical therapy without benefit and ultimately came to a subacromion decompression in November 2002.  She had ongoing pain and was evaluated by Dr. X who felt that she had a possible brachial plexopathy.  He also felt she had a right superficial radial neuritis and blocked this with resolution of her symptoms.  He then referred her to ABCD who did EMG testing, demonstrating a right suprascapular neuropathy although a C5 radiculopathy could not be ruled out.  MRI testing on the cervical spine was then done which was negative for disk herniation and she underwent suprascapular nerve decompression of the scapular notch on 12/18/03.  She finally went to an anterior axillary nerve block because of ongoing pain in the anterior shoulder again by Dr. X.  She comes to me for impairment rating.  She has no chronic health problems otherwise, fevers, chills, or general malaise.  She is not working.  She is right-hand dominant.  She denies any prior history of injury to her shoulder.,PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:,  Negative aside from above.,FAMILY HISTORY: , Noncontributory.,SOCIAL HISTORY:  ,Please see above.,REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:,  Negative aside from above.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  ,A pleasant, age appropriate woman, moderately overweight, in no apparent distress.  Normal gait and station, normal posture, normal strength, tone, sensation and deep tendon reflexes with the exception of 4+/5 strength in the supraspinatus musculature on the right.  She has decreased motion in the right shoulder as follows.  She has 160 degrees of flexion, 155 degrees of abduction, 35 degrees of extension, 25 degrees of adduction, 45 degrees of internal rotation and 90 degrees of external rotation.  She has a positive impingement sign on the right.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT:,  Right shoulder impingement syndrome, right suprascapular neuropathy.,DISCUSSION: , With a reasonable degree of medical certainty, she is at maximum medical improvement and she does have an impairment based on AMA Guide to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, Fifth Edition.  The reason for this impairment is the incident of 01/01/02.  For her suprascapular neuropathy, she is rated as a grade IV motor deficit which I rate as a 13% motor deficit.  This is multiplied by a maximum upper extremity impairment for involvement of the suprascapular nerve of 16% which produces a 2% impairment of the upper extremity when the two values are multiplied together, 2% impairment of the upper extremity.  For her lack of motion in the shoulder she also has additional impairment on the right.  She has a 1% impairment of the upper extremity due to lack of shoulder flexion.  She has a 1% impairment of the upper extremity due to lack of shoulder abduction.  She has a 1% impairment of the upper extremity due to lack of shoulder adduction.  She has a 1% impairment of the upper extremity due to lack of shoulder extension.  There is no impairment for findings in shoulder external rotation.  She has a 3% impairment of the upper extremity due to lack of shoulder internal rotation.  Thus the impairment due to lack of motion in her shoulder is a 6% impairment of the upper extremity.  This combines with the 2% impairment of the upper extremity due to weakness in the suprascapular nerve root distribution to produce an 8% impairment of the upper extremity which in turn is a 5% impairment of the whole person based on the AMA Guide to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, Fifth Edition, stated with a reasonable degree of medical certainty.
human_dx_summary: The patient has right shoulder impingement syndrome and right suprascapular neuropathy resulting in a combined 8% upper extremity impairment and 5% whole person impairment based on AMA guidelines.

**ASSESSMENT:**  
Chronic right shoulder pain and dysfunction status post work-related injury (01/01/02) with subacromial decompression (11/2002), right superficial radial nerve block, suprascapular nerve decompression at spinoglenoid notch (12/18/03), and anterior axillary nerve block. Persistent 4+/5 supraspinatus strength deficit (suprascapular nerve distribution) with mildly reduced active ROM (notably internal rotation) and positive Neer impingement sign, consistent with residual post-surgical changes, incomplete suprascapular nerve recovery, and/or recurrent subacromial impingement ± rotator cuff pathology. No evidence of cervical radiculopathy (prior negative MRI/EMG). No red flags for infection, inflammatory arthropathy, or neoplasm. Whole person impairment rating: 8% (5% upper extremity impairment for strength/ROM deficits per AMA Guides 5th Ed., converted; causal relationship to index injury supported by history/exam).

**PLAN:**  
1. **Impairment rating:** Completed today as above; report forwarded to referring agency/insurer.  
2. **Imaging:** Order right shoulder MRI (non-contrast) to evaluate rotator cuff integrity, residual suprascapular nerve entrapment, and acromial morphology.  
3. **Medications:**  
   - Ibuprofen 600 mg PO q8h prn pain (max 2400 mg/day, take with food; 30 tabs, #1).  
   - Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg PO qHS prn spasm (14 tabs, #1).  
4. **Therapy:** PT referral for shoulder ROM/strengthening (supraspinatus/scapular stabilization focus, 2x/week x 6 weeks); trial subacromial corticosteroid injection if PT fails.  
5. **Referrals:** Orthopedics (shoulder specialist) for surgical opinion re: possible revision decompression/rotator cuff repair.  
6. **Follow-up:** Return in 4 weeks or sooner if worsening pain/weakness; RTC post-MRI. Off work until re-evaluated. Patient educated on activity modification (no overhead lifting >5 lbs), home exercises, and red flags (fever, progressive weakness).

**ASSESSMENT:**  
1. **Acute decompensated systolic heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV), recurrent post recent hospitalization** – Patient with known nonischemic cardiomyopathy and prior CHF exacerbation presents with persistent SOB at rest/exertion, orthopnea, PND, 6 lb weight gain, JVD (5 cm), S3/S4 gallop, hepatomegaly (5 cm below costal margin), and 1+ LE edema, consistent with biventricular congestion despite clear lungs (no overt pulmonary edema). Primary etiology: medication non-adherence (failed to fill discharge prescriptions with increased doses) and recent cocaine use (toxicology + on 01/08 hospitalization), both known precipitants of decompensation via increased sympathetic drive, afterload, and negative inotropy. Tachycardia (HR 91) and uncontrolled HTN further contribute.  
2. **Hypertensive urgency** – BP 151-152/102-104 mmHg, non-adherent to home regimen, exacerbating HF.  
3. **Hepatic congestion secondary to right heart failure, ? early cirrhotic changes from Hepatitis C** – New RUQ pain, nausea, anorexia, and hepatomegaly in setting of passive congestion; Hep C history warrants exclusion of active viral flare or decompensation.  
4. **History of NSVT and branch vessel CAD** – Stable clinically (no palpitations/syncope), but warrants surveillance given acute decompensation.  

**PLAN:**  
1. **Hospital admission** – Admit to telemetry floor for close monitoring, IV diuresis, and HF optimization (SOB at rest, JVD, organ congestion warrant inpatient management to avoid further deterioration).  
   - **Labs:** STAT CBC, CMP (renal/hepatic function, electrolytes), BNP, troponin, TSH, lipid panel; Hep C viral load/genotype if >6 months old; INR/PT.  
   - **Imaging:** CXR (baseline for congestion/effusion); TTE (assess EF, RV function, valves if not done since last admission).  
   - **ECG** – Rhythm, ischemia/strain.  
2. **Medications (initiate inpatient):**  
   - **Diuresis:** Furosemide 40 mg IV q12h (titrate to -1-2 kg/day UOP, goal dry weight ~166 lbs); consider metolazone 2.5-5 mg PO if poor response.  
   - **HF optimization:** Restart/increase GDMT per inpatient protocol – e.g., lisinopril 10-20 mg daily (titrate after BP control), metoprolol succinate 25-50 mg daily (titrate HR goal 55-60), spironolactone 25 mg daily (if K+ <5.0).  
   - **HTN:** Hold ACEI initially if Cr rising; add hydralazine 25 mg TID if needed.  
   - Continue statin (e.g., atorvastatin 40-80 mg) and antiplatelet (e.g., aspirin 81 mg) from prior regimen.  
   - Pain/nausea: Acetaminophen 500 mg q6h PRN (avoid NSAIDs).  
3. **Consults:**  
   - **Cardiology** – Urgent for GDMT titration, NSVT management (consider ICD if EF <35% and not already placed).  
   - **Hepatology/GI** – Outpatient if LFTs stable post-diuresis, for Hep C evaluation/treatment candidacy.  
4. **Lifestyle/education:** Strict low-sodium (<2g/day) diet, daily weights, med adherence counseling (provide 7-day bridge prescriptions on DC). Substance abuse counseling for cocaine cessation (urine tox screen inpatient); smoking cessation reinforced.  
5. **Follow-up:** Clinic return 7-10 days post-discharge (or sooner if readmit); telehealth for weight/BP logs. Advance to GDMT target doses as outpatient.

He did windup taking Benadryl at that time.  He has not taken anything today for his symptoms, but he is on hydrochlorothiazide and metoprolol for hypertension as well as a baby aspirin each day.,ALLERGIES: , HE DOES HAVE MEDICATION INTOLERANCES TO SULFA DRUGS (HEADACHE), MORPHINE (NAUSEA AND VOMITING), AND TORADOL (ULCER).,SOCIAL HISTORY: , Patient is married and is a nonsmoker and lives with his wife, who is here with him.,Nursing notes were reviewed with which I agree.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION,VITAL SIGNS:  Temp and vital signs are all within normal limits.,GENERAL:  In general, the patient is an elderly white male who is sitting on the stretcher in no acute distress.,HEENT:  Head is normocephalic and atraumatic.  The face shows no edema.  The tongue is not swollen and the airway is widely patent.,NECK:  No stridor.,HEART:  Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.,LUNGS:  Clear without rales, rhonchi, or wheezes.,EXTREMITIES:  Upper extremities, there is some edema and erythema to the dorsum of the left hand in the region of the distal third to fifth metacarpals. llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT:**  
76-year-old male with localized reaction to bee sting (hymenoptera envenomation) on the dorsum of the left hand. Clinical reasoning: Patient reports multiple stings today with isolated progressive erythema and edema confined to the left hand (distal 3rd-5th metacarpals and 4th digit) without systemic symptoms (e.g., urticaria, dyspnea, angioedema, or anaphylaxis). Prior bee sting 1 month ago with minimal reaction treated with diphenhydramine. Exam confirms focal findings without lymphadenopathy, lymphangitis, fever, or signs of secondary infection/cellulitis. No evidence of anaphylaxis despite beta-blocker use (metoprolol), which increases risk but is not manifest here. Elderly patient with HTN on standard therapy; low concern for tetanus given puncture nature without devitalized tissue.

**PLAN:**  
1. **Symptomatic management:**  
   - Elevate left hand above heart level as much as possible.  
   - Cool compresses/ice packs 20 min on/off PRN for swelling/pain.  
   - Antihistamine: Loratadine (Claritin) 10 mg PO daily x 3-5 days (first dose given in office). May add diphenhydramine 25-50 mg PO q6h PRN if itching worsens (used successfully previously).  
   - Analgesia: Acetaminophen 650-1000 mg PO q6h PRN (max 3 g/day); avoid NSAIDs due to Toradol intolerance/ulcer history.  

2. **Wound care:** Keep site clean/dry; no dressing needed. Monitor for progression.  

3. **No additional laboratory tests or imaging** at this time (low-risk local reaction; no systemic signs, fever, or concerning exam findings).  

4. **No procedures, referrals, or consultations** needed.  

5. **Return precautions:** RTC urgently (same day) or to ED if worsening redness/swelling beyond hand, increasing pain, fever >100.4°F, red streaking, pus/drainage, numbness, systemic symptoms (hives, SOB, throat tightness), or inability to use hand.  

6. **Follow-up:** Phone check-in or RTC in clinic 48-72 hours or sooner PRN. Continue HTN meds (HCTZ, metoprolol, ASA); no changes. Education provided to patient and wife on local reaction course (may peak 24-48 hours).

llm_dx_summary: 76-year-old male presenting with a localized erythematous and edematous reaction to multiple bee stings on the left hand without systemic symptoms or signs of infection.

Her husband left around 7 in the morning and returned around 11 and found her sleeping.  About 30 minutes after his arrival, he found the empty bottles and woke up the patient to bring her to the hospital.,She says she wishes she would have died, but is happy she is alive and is currently not suicidal because she notes her sons may be have to be tested for the Huntington gene. ### ASSESSMENT:
53-year-old female with history of malignant melanoma s/p resection and lymphadenectomy (2008) presenting with acute left basicervical femoral neck fracture (high intertrochanteric/basicervical pattern, lesser trochanter intact) after low-energy twisting injury while ambulating with walker. Likely **pathologic fracture** given presence of lytic lesion adjacent to femoral neck on limited X-ray, prior melanoma with lymphatic spread, and subacute preceding back/left leg pain suggestive of possible metastatic disease (vs. insufficiency fracture from chronic sciatica). No acute neurologic deficits. Differential for lytic lesion includes metastatic melanoma (most likely), myeloma, or other primary bone malignancy; benign etiology (e.g., geode) less likely given history/clinical context. Chronic sciatica/back pain may represent metastatic spinal disease.

### PLAN:
1. **Admission**: Admit to Orthopedic service for surgical management and metastatic workup.
2. **Imaging**:
   - STAT repeat X-rays: AP/lateral pelvis, full left femur (hip to knee), and left knee to better characterize fracture pattern, displacement, and lytic lesion.
   - STAT CT left hip/pelvis with reconstructions to delineate fracture morphology, lytic lesion extent, and cortical involvement.
   - MRI lumbosacral spine (non-contrast if renal concerns) to evaluate for spinal metastases given back pain history.
   - Whole-body PET/CT or Tc-99m bone scan (PET preferred for melanoma staging) within 24-48 hours to assess for additional osseous/soft tissue metastases.
3. **Laboratory tests**:
   - STAT CBC, CMP (incl. calcium, albumin), PT/INR, LDH (melanoma marker), ESR/CRP.
   - SPEP/UPEP with immunofixation if lytic lesion suggestive of myeloma.
4. **Surgical intervention**:
   - Urgent orthopedic surgery consult (already in place): Recommend ORIF with cephalomedullary nail if purely basicervical and limited mets; consider proximal femoral replacement (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty) given pathologic nature and patient age. Biopsy lytic lesion intraoperatively if feasible. Discuss goals of care, risks (infection, nonunion, progression of mets), and alternatives (nonoperative, though poor given pain/unweightbearing).
   - NPO after midnight; type/screen 2 units PRBC.
5. **Medications**:
   - Pain control: IV hydromorphone 0.5-1 mg q3-4h PRN breakthrough (hold if sedated); transition to oxycodone-acetaminophen 5-10/325 mg PO q6h PRN post-op. Multimodal: scheduled acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h, gabapentin 100-300 mg PO TID for neuropathic component.
   - DVT prophylaxis: Enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily (if CrCl >30; adjust if renal impairment) or sequential compression devices if high bleed risk.
   - Hold NSAIDs until cleared.
6. **Consultations**:
   - Medical Oncology: Urgent, for metastatic melanoma workup/staging and perioperative systemic therapy discussion (e.g., immunotherapy if BRAF+).
   - Pain Management: If refractory post-op pain.
7. **Procedures**: Intraoperative biopsy/cultures of lytic lesion if indicated.
8. **Follow-up**:
   - Daily inpatient ortho rounds until discharge.
   - Outpatient ortho f/u 2 weeks post-op (or sooner if discharged early) with X-rays.
   - Oncology f/u within 1 week post-staging imaging.
   - PT/OT starting post-op day 1 with hip precautions/weightbearing as tolerated per surgical fixation.

**Code status**: Full code (discuss if advanced disease). Patient counseled on pathologic fracture suspicion and need for staging; verbal consent obtained for imaging/surgery.

Symptoms of "drainage" per daughter consistent with chronic/recurrent UTIs; may be stroke mimic or concurrent stressor.
3. **Uncontrolled hyperglycemia**: Glucose 220 on insulin regimen (Lantus/SS); exacerbating stroke risk.
4. **Severe aortic stenosis**: 4/6 SEM with carotid radiation; embolic source for stroke. Known PMH.
5. **CKD stage 3 (baseline)**: Cr 1.3, BUN 52; monitor with nephrotoxins.
6. **Nonspecific EKG changes**: Mild diffuse ST depression/biphasic T waves; ?demand ischemia vs electrolyte/repolarization abnormality.

### PLAN:
1. **Acute stroke management**:
   - Await stat non-contrast head CT results (pending). If no hemorrhage/mass effect and symptom onset <4.5 hours, IV alteplase (tPA) 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg; 10% bolus, 90% infusion over 60 min) per stroke protocol after NIHSS (estimate 8-12). Notify stroke team/neurology STAT for activation.
   - Admit to stroke unit/ICU for neuro checks q1h initially.
   - Permissive HTN (target <185/110 pre-tPA, <180/105 post; hold Lopressor if needed).
   - Aspirin 325 mg PO/NG stat (hold if tPA given, start 24h post).
   - High-intensity statin: atorvastatin 80 mg PO nightly (check lipids if time permits).
   - Neurology consult STAT for NIHSS, tPA eligibility, and further workup (e.g., CTA head/neck if no tPA).

2. **UTI treatment**:
   - Ciprofloxacin 250 mg PO BID x 7 days (CrCl ~40-50 mL/min based on Cr 1.3/elderly; dose-adjusted) OR ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h if systemic sx worsen. Urine culture/sens pending; narrow Abx once results.
   - Increase fluids; monitor output.

3. **DM/Glucose control**:
   - Insulin sliding scale per protocol; increase Lantus to 40 units qHS if persistent >180.
   - Accuchecks q4-6h; target 140-180.

4. **Supportive**:
   - IVF: NS at 75 mL/hr (monitor for fluid overload given AS/CHF hx).
   - Pain: Continue Lortab PRN; hold Ativan (sedation risk in acute stroke).
   - DVT ppx: SCDs (bilat BKA); consider heparin 5000 U SQ BID if mobile.
   - Swallow screen prior to PO; speech therapy eval.
   - Echo (TTE) today to assess AS/valve (embolic source?).

5. **Workup**:
   - Labs: CBC, CMP, troponin, lipids, HbA1c, ESR/CRP today; coags/lactate if tPA.
   - EKG q8h x3; telemetry.
   - If CT negative/equivocal: MRI brain.

6. **Follow-up**: Neuro checks q1-2h x24h then q4h. F/U with daughter re: goals of care/code status (discuss hospice if poor prognosis). DC to rehab/SNF once stable (3-5 days). Neurology f/u in 1 week post-DC.

### ASSESSMENT:
28-year-old right-hand dominant male with ulnar-sided right hand pain after punching a wall 3 days ago, consistent with a high-energy axial load injury. ER evaluation showed carpometacarpal (CMC) dislocations of the 3rd and 4th metacarpals, which were manually reduced. Current exam reveals persistent swelling and tenderness over the ulnar dorsum, with preserved ROM, strength, sensation, and vascularity. Today's radiographs demonstrate possible small avulsion fractures at the bases of the 3rd and 4th metacarpals, with confirmed adduction deformity at the 4th and 5th CMC joints suggestive of incomplete reduction, residual subluxation, or instability. No evidence of acute compartment syndrome, nerve/vascular injury, or infection. Differential includes fracture-dislocations of the 3rd-5th CMC joints (boxer's CMC injury), with low concern for extensor tendon injury given intact cascade and extension.

### PLAN:
1. **Orthopedics/Hand Surgery Referral**: Urgent outpatient referral to hand surgeon today for evaluation of CMC stability (3rd-5th metacarpals); these injuries often require stress views, CT, or surgical fixation (e.g., K-wires) if unstable.
2. **Imaging**:
   - CT right hand (with 3D reconstructions) to better delineate fractures, CMC alignment, and intra-articular involvement.
   - Consider dynamic fluoroscopy or stress views in ortho clinic if not done emergently.
3. **Immobilization**: Continue ulnar gutter splint (MCP joints in 70-90° flexion) full-time x 2 weeks; no removal for hygiene until ortho eval. Educate on splint care and elevation.
4. **Medications**:
   - Ibuprofen 600 mg PO q6-8h PRN pain (max 2400 mg/day) x 7 days.
   - Acetaminophen 1000 mg PO q6h PRN pain, alternating with ibuprofen.
5. **Activity**: Strict hand rest—no weightbearing, gripping, or use of right hand. Ice 20 min q2-4h PRN.
6. **Follow-up**: Return to clinic in 2-3 days if worsening pain, swelling, numbness, or inability to extend fingers. Otherwise, f/u with hand surgery within 48-72 hours; clinic f/u 1 week post-ortho eval or sooner if needed.
7. **Patient Education**: Discuss mechanism, risks of malunion/nonunion if unstable (stiffness, pain, weakness), importance of compliance. No labs needed. RTC PRN.

### ASSESSMENT:
85-year-old female with acute onset diarrhea, vomiting, and epigastric abdominal pain, most consistent with **acute gastroenteritis (likely infectious/viral)** complicated by **dehydration and prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI)**.  
**Clinical reasoning**: History of vomiting/diarrhea with exam findings of dry oropharynx and mild epigastric tenderness (no peritonitis). Labs show prerenal azotemia (BUN:Cr ratio ~24:1, BUN 54, Cr 2.2 from presumed baseline), high anion gap metabolic acidosis (AG=20), mild hypokalemia (K 3.3), and hyperglycemia (glc 165). Normal WBC, afebrile status, and normoactive BS argue against complicated intra-abdominal process (e.g., acute diverticulitis, though history of diverticulosis noted). No evidence of ischemia or obstruction. Prolonged QT interval likely secondary to electrolyte derangements/hypokalemia (monitor; less likely Lexapro). Poor historian limits details but no red flags for alternative etiology (e.g., ACS ruled out by negative troponin/EKG beyond QT).

### PLAN:
1. **Admission**: Admit to Medicine floor for IV hydration and monitoring (high fall/ delirium risk in elderly with AKI/hearing impairment; obtain family collateral history).
2. **IV Fluids**: NS 1L bolus x1, then D5 1/2NS + 20mEq KCl at 100-125mL/hr; recheck electrolytes q6-8h and adjust (goal: euvolemia, Cr improvement, K>3.5).
3. **Medications**:
   - Ondansetron 4mg IV q8h PRN nausea/vomiting.
   - Hold lorazepam/Tylenol PM (sedation risk contributing to presentation).
   - Continue home meds (Lexapro, Klor-Con, Ca/Vit D) unless contraindicated; hold if volume overloaded.
   - No empiric antibiotics (low suspicion for bacterial process).
4. **Laboratory tests**:
   - Repeat CMP, Mg, phos q12h x2.
   - Serum lactate, blood cultures x2 if fever develops.
   - Stool studies: C. difficile toxin, fecal WBC, stool culture/ova & parasites.
5. **Imaging studies**: Abdominal flat/pillow view (rule out obstruction/ileus); CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast if no Cr improvement in 24h or worsening pain/fever (evaluate for diverticulitis/abscess).
6. **Consultations**: None urgently; Renal if Cr rises >0.3 or persistent despite fluids.
7. **Procedures**: None.
8. **Follow-up plan**: Daily inpatient reassessment; discharge when tolerating PO, electrolytes normalized, pain resolved (est. 2-3 days); PCP f/u in 1 week with repeat Cr; audiology/social work for hearing/communication aids if family identifies need. Education on hydration, diet (BRAT), and med reconciliation.

**ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:**

**1. Acute left lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), confirmed on Doppler ultrasound.**  
This is a new diagnosis in the setting of active systemic chemotherapy (paclitaxel/carboplatin) for stage IIIC papillary serous ovarian carcinoma, a known hypercoagulable state predisposing to venous thromboembolism (VTE). No clinical evidence of pulmonary embolism (PE) at this time (no dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxia, or EKG changes). Local exam findings (swelling, erythema, warmth, tenderness) are consistent with DVT without signs of cellulitis or abscess. Elevated WBC with neutrophilia likely reflects inflammation from DVT and/or chemotherapy effects rather than infection (afebrile, no systemic signs).

**2. Stage IIIC papillary serous ovarian adenocarcinoma, s/p staging surgery, currently on cycle 1 day 14/21 of paclitaxel/carboplatin.**  
Neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy course ongoing; IP port placement scheduled next week. No interval progression or complications noted today.

**3. Mild chemotherapy-related anemia (Hgb 11.4) and leukocytosis (WBC 15.5).**  
Expected on current regimen; platelets preserved.

**4. Mild hypokalemia (K 3.3) and hyperglycemia (glucose 152).**  
Likely chemotherapy-related electrolyte shift and stress response; no prior diabetes.

**PLAN:**  
**Immediate management of DVT:**  
- Initiate **therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)**: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously BID (target weight-based dosing; confirm weight at next visit for precise calculation, e.g., ~90 mg BID if ~90 kg). Continue for at least 3-6 months or duration of chemotherapy, per NCCN guidelines for cancer-associated thrombosis. Transition to outpatient hematology for long-term management (LMWH or DOAC consideration).  
- **No warfarin/DOAC initiation** at this time due to cancer-associated VTE preference for LMWH.  
- Leg elevation while supine; trial **graduated compression stockings (20-30 mmHg)** on right leg and contralateral to DVT once acute swelling improves (avoid initially on affected leg to prevent propagation).  
- Pain control: Continue **tramadol 50 mg PO q6h PRN**; add **ibuprofen 600 mg PO q6-8h PRN** if no contraindication (monitor renal function).  

**Chemotherapy/oncology coordination:**  
- Notify gynecologic oncology re: DVT diagnosis; confirm plan for IP port placement next week (proceed if stable; hold chemo if bleeding concerns). Complete current cycle if ANC >1000 (currently preserved).  

**Workup:**  
- **D-dimer**: Stat to confirm VTE burden (not essential for management but for baseline).  
- **CTA chest with PE protocol**: If any new respiratory symptoms develop; defer for now given stability.  
- **Repeat CBC with diff, CMP, PT/PTT/INR**: In 48-72 hours to monitor for anticoagulation response, myelosuppression, and electrolytes.  

**Referrals/consults:**  
- **Hematology**: Urgent outpatient referral for VTE management in cancer patient (appt within 1 week).  
- Gynecologic oncology: Already engaged; f/u as scheduled.  

**Follow-up:**  
- Return to clinic in 48-72 hours for repeat exam/labs and enoxaparin teaching (self-injection). Then q1-2 weeks with oncology/heme.  
- Patient education: Signs of bleeding/PE (dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest pain), injection technique, avoid NSAIDs if bleeding risk rises. Call 911 for emergencies.  
- Lifestyle: Maintain ambulation, hydration; no travel until anticoagulated x48h.  

Prognosis favorable with prompt anticoagulation; continue surveillance for ovarian ca recurrence/response to therapy.
